See what's inside\n22\tgribtract list hrrr.t00z.wrfsfcf01.grib2\n23\t\n24\t# 4. Decode everything to JSON\n25\tgribtract decode hrrr.t00z.wrfsfcf01.grib2\n26\t```\n27\t\n28\t> **⚠️ CLI not yet implemented** — The commands above (steps 1, 3, 4) document the planned interface but are not yet functional. It's the primary output format for **GFS, HRRR, NBM, GEFS, NAM**, and similar numerical weather prediction products.\n56\t\n57\tDecoding it means handling multi-section message framing, four grid geometries, parameter tables indexed by discipline/category/number, five data-packing algorithms, and bitmaps for missing-value masking.\n58\t\n59\tThe standard tools (`wgrib2`, `eccodes`) are C programs. If you need decoded GRIB2 values in a Rust project, your options were: shell out, bind through FFI, or give up and parse bytes yourself.\n60\t\n61\t**gribtract is the native Rust alternative.**\n62\t\n63\t## ✨ Features\n64\t\n65\t- 🦀 **Pure Rust core** — no C toolchain or FFI for simple, complex, complex+spatial-differencing, and PNG packing (DRT 5.0 / 5.2 / 5.3 / 5.41); JPEG2000 (5.40) available behind the optional `jpeg2000` feature\n66\t- 🏷️ **Typed output** — every decoded field carries structured metadata: parameter ID, level, forecast time, grid geometry\n67\t- 🗺️ **Four grid projections** — lat/lon (GDT 3.0), polar stereographic (3.20), Lambert conformal (3.30), Gaussian (3.40)\n68\t- ⚡ **Lazy decode path** — parse headers only, defer grid data; extract single grid points in **O(1)** for DRT=0 fields without decoding the full grid\n69\t- 📈 **Timeseries extractor** — pull per-station forecast series for a list of lat/lon coordinates in one call\n70\t- 🌐 **Byte-range fetching** — `gribtract-fetch` downloads GRIB2 (or slices of it) from NOAA S3, GCS, and NOMADS over HTTP range requests\n71\t- 🐍 **Python bindings** — `gribtract-py` (PyO3) exposes the decoder to Python\n72\t- ✅ **Oracle-gated correctness** — every release is verified against eccodes/wgrib2 over a corpus of real NOAA files; It's the primary output format for **GFS, HRRR, NBM, GEFS, NAM**, and similar numerical weather prediction products.\n\nDecoding it means handling multi-section message framing, four grid geometries, parameter tables indexed by discipline/category/number, five data-packing algorithms, and bitmaps for missing-value masking.\n\nThe standard tools (`wgrib2`, `eccodes`) are C programs. If you need decoded GRIB2 values in a Rust project, your options were: shell out, bind through FFI, or give up and parse bytes yourself.\n\n**gribtract is the native Rust alternative.**\n\n## ✨ Features\n\n- 🦀 **Pure Rust core** — no C toolchain or FFI for simple, complex, complex+spatial-differencing, and PNG packing (DRT 5.0 / 5.2 / 5.3 / 5.41); JPEG2000 (5.40) available behind the optional `jpeg2000` feature\n- 🏷️ **Typed output** — every decoded field carries structured metadata: parameter ID, level, forecast time, grid geometry\n- 🗺️ **Four grid projections** — lat/lon (GDT 3.0), polar stereographic (3.20), Lambert conformal (3.30), Gaussian (3.40)\n- ⚡ **Lazy decode path** — parse headers only, defer grid data; extract single grid points in **O(1)** for DRT=0 fields without decoding the full grid\n- 📈 **Timeseries extractor** — pull per-station forecast series for a list of lat/lon coordinates in one call\n- 🌐 **Byte-range fetching** — `gribtract-fetch` downloads GRIB2 (or slices of it) from NOAA S3, GCS, and NOMADS over HTTP range requests\n- 🐍 **Python bindings** — `gribtract-py` (PyO3) exposes the decoder to Python\n- ✅ **Oracle-gated correctness** — every release is verified against eccodes/wgrib2 over a corpus of real NOAA files; agreement can only ratchet up\n\n## 🌍 Geographic Coverage\n\ngribtract provides comprehensive coverage for CONUS (Continental United States) weather station data extraction, validated against real NOAA HRRR CONUS GRIB2 files.\n\n### Validated Coverage Areas\n\n**CONUS Coverage:** ✅ **100% station coverage confirmed** (56/56 stations tested)\n\nThe HRRR CONUS grid (Lambert Conformal Conic, 3km resolution) covers:\n- **Northern extent:** 48.57°N (International Falls, MN)\n- **Southern extent:** 25.91°N (Brownsville, TX) \n- **Western extent:** 122.60°W (Portland, OR)\n- **Eastern extent:** 71.01°W (Boston, MA)\n\n### Station Coverage by Region\n\n| Region | Stations | Coverage | Notes |\n|--------|----------|----------|-------|\n| East Coast | 5 | 100% | 4 marginal stations near grid edge |\n| Southeast | 8 | 100% | Florida peninsula covered |\n| Midwest | 8 | 100% | Excellent coverage, no edge issues |\n| South Central | 7 | 100% | Well-covered region |\n| Mountain | 4 | 100% | No coverage gaps |\n| West Coast | 8 | 100% | 7 marginal stations near grid edge |\n| Southwest | 4 | 100% | Good coverage |\n| Northern Border | 6 | 100% | Complete border coverage |\n| Southern Border | 5 | 100% | Complete border coverage |\n\n### Geographic Limitations\n\n⚠️ **Edge Proximity:** ~27% of tested stations are within 100 km of grid boundaries, particularly:\n- **West Coast stations:** Seattle, Portland, San Francisco, Los Angeles (near eastern grid edge)\n- **East Coast stations:** Boston, New York, Philadelphia (near western grid edge)\n- **Florida stations:** Miami, Ft.
